subject: Parameterizing nested hierarchy in survival model, fixed/random effects

messages.author: b5f4802dc12ec04d
messages.subject: Parameterizing nested hierarchy in survival model, fixed/random effects
parts:
Hi all,

I'm working on modeling nest survival and running into a hierarchy parameterization question. Implementing with JAGS. 

The dataset in question includes:
- 7 sites 
- 2 regions (2 sites in one region, 5 in the other)
- 2 years (data from all sites in both years, n ranging 5-80 per year/site combo)

When I've run models before, I treat site as a random effect (random intercept?) like so:

model {
#Priors and linear models
for (s in 1:7) {
phi.site[s] ~ dlogis(3.5, 0.75)
}
#Likelihood
for (i in 1:n.nest) {
for (t in (f[i]+1):k[i]) {
logit(phi[i,t-1]) <- phi.site[site[i]]
y[i,t] ~ dbern(phi[i,t-1] * y[i,t-1])

} #t
} #i
#derived parameter: nest success
for (ns in 1:7) {
nest.succ[ns] <- ilogit(phi.site[ns])^nestperiod
}
}

To include year as a random effect, I did:
model {
#Priors and linear models
for (y in 1:2) {
for (s in 1:7) {
phi.year.site[y,s] ~ dlogis(3.5, 0.75)
}
}
#Likelihood
for (i in 1:n.nest) {
for (t in (f[i]+1):k[i]) {
logit(phi[i,t-1]) <- phi.year.site[year[i], site[i]]
y[i,t] ~ dbern(phi[i,t-1] * y[i,t-1])

} #t
} #i
#derived parameter: nest success
for (y in 1:2) {
for (s in 1:7) {
nest.succ[y,s] <- ilogit(phi.year.site[y,s])^nestperiod
}
}
}

Is this correct parameterization? I get a unique value of nest survival for each year/site combination. And I could post-hoc infer differences in nest survival across years and sites by the overlap of the credible intervals?

But there are 2 regions, which are two distinct non-interbreeding populations, and I feel ignoring that as in the above structure, is not correct. But trying to add region as a 3rd dimension to the for loop above doesn't work for me (different numbers of sites per region) and also doesn't make sense, unless I somehow get an output of a mean at the region level, and an estimate at each site. From a conservation objective perspective, the unit that managers are most interested in would include site, because of specific management actions that are happening at each site. But how can I account for region and site and year in the same model? Instead of a random intercept for each site, would it be a region random effect, and then a slope coefficient for each level of site that is different than the "reference" category for region?

Other predictors I would like to include are a linear and quadratic effect of egg initiation date, and age of nest, which could also be parameterized as a random slope, allowing the effect of the linear predictor to vary at whichever level of random effects makes the most sense (unique slope for site and year?)

I feel like this is relatively basic modeling 101 fixed vs random effects parameterization that I'm struggling to parse out in this scenario and apply to my JAGS code; any advice would be appreciated.

Thank you,

Stephanie

messages.author: 8cfa39771ad4bc4f
messages.subject: Re: Parameterizing nested hierarchy in survival model, fixed/random effects
parts:
Hi Stephanie,

I'll take a crack at this! So a couple thoughts:

I do think this is a 'fixed vs. random effect' question, and it could help to think about what those things are and how they are often used. Sometimes you can treat an X-variable as either a fixed or random effect, but it depends on what you are trying to accomplish with that variable and there may be advantages/disadvantages to either approach.

I was taught that fixed effects are things that influences averages, they represent main hypotheses you want to test, and they may have a limited number of groups. On the other hand, random effects are sources of variation, they may influence variation around averages, and you want to account for this variation while perhaps testing other main hypotheses of interest. A random effect may have many, many groups (>6 is the threshold that I teach; I think Ben Bolker says ~8). Maybe the most important consideration is: are you interested in how the x-variable influences the mean, or how the x-variable influences variation? OK, but what the heck exactly do these terms mean with respect to math in a statistical model?

A fixed effect is something that influences the mean outcome. If you are modeling true survival (S) with a binomial, logistic-regression model, then: logit(S) = beta0 + beta1*X1 + epsilon_residual ~ N(0, sigma_residual). In this model, survival is constrained to be between 0-1 (logit-link function), and then modeled with a linear model with an intercept (beta0; the average survival when all x-variables are zero), plus beta1*X1 (the effect of the X-variable), plus residual error that is normally distributed with a mean of zero and a standard deviation, sigma. So survival can get bigger or smaller with the x-variable, and then there is residual error (epsilon) that is un-explained. Which we always have in nature. 

Alternatively, a random-effects model would instead add an additional error term(s) to this equation, e.g.: logit(S) = beta0 + epsilon_x1 ~ N(0, sigma_x1) + epsilon_residual ~ N(0, sigma_residual). Your x-variable is now another source of error, that is normally distributed with a mean of zero and a standard deviation, sigma_x1; you are now saying there is random variation around a mean of zero, with a standard deviation due to that X-variable. And then residual error still in the equation too. You now have to estimate a standard deviation for your x-variable, which requires ~samples; and this is why you need many, many samples for the random effect (above). Note, you need more than one measurement within each level of your random effect, which will allow you to measure and partition error due to the random effect as different from your residual error.

Now, you might want to include both fixed and random effects in a model, and you can do that! This is called a mixed-effects model: e.g., logit(S) = beta0 + beta1*X1 + epsilon_random ~ N(0, sigma_random) + epsilon_residual ~ N(0, sigma_residual).

So the reason why I am diving into the math is... because in your first model you showed, I do not think the site effect is a random effect, and instead I believe you are treating site as a fixed-effect. You are saying each site, s, from 1:7, has a different mean survival. These means are different, and while you are not measuring differences between those means, you could. And as such I believe you are treating these as fixed effects. If you wanted to treat site as a random effect, I believe you would need to model survival among sites as a random variable that might be normally distributed with a mean of zero and a standard deviation -- and you would estimate that standard deviation in your model. It would use your data from each site to estimate the most likely survival values for each site, and characterize the shape/distribution of that distribution among sites with a standard deviation/variance/tau. I do not see that in either of your models. 

It's been awhile since I pawed through Marc and Michael's (incredible) books, but my memory is that, for your site effect in both models, they call this a 'means parameterization'. As you noted, this will give you different mean values for your groups (in this case, sites in your first model, or site-by-year in your second model) -- but my understanding is these are fixed effects. An alternative approach might be to use an 'effects parameterization', where you specify a linear model with different effects (like above: beta0 + beta1*X1 + ... + error); this makes it more ~apparent that you are modeling fixed effects. But it becomes impractical when you have many groups (like you do). 

Should you change this to treat site as a random effect? I am not sure, but you are wise to consider it. You have many sites, it would be impractical to treat them all as fixed effects with the effects parameterization I described above. However, your current 'means paramerertization' approach is pretty concise. However, you are treating each site (or site-by-year combo) as a different event in your models. While it will estimate each site as different (as you noted), it does not allow information sharing among sites. Instead, a random effect would pool all the information and share information to characterize the overall mean, variation among sites. With 7 sites (or 14 site-year combos), this might be more powerful and result in less uncertainty in your estimates. Either a fixed or random treatment will result in different estimates for your sites and years, which is the information that you appear most keen on. And you are correct that you can compare the medians (95% HPD) to infer if they are different. So either approach might work, although the resulting uncertainty might be different. You would likely want whichever one has less uncertainty! 

It seem like you have 2 regions, and you maybe suspect/hypothesize that regional effect to be important at influencing overall means. With only 2 regions, I would treat it as a fixed effect. I believe this would not require a third dimension to your array, which is good! Because three-dimensional arrays hurt the brain. Instead, use a 'region' variable from your dataframe for each nest, and then add this as a fixed effect into your linear model for logit(phi[i,t-1]), on the right-hand side. beta_region*region[x]. It will likely require some indexing relative to your regions/sites/nests, but it can be done. 

Now, for year, you only have 2 years. What do you think, fixed or random? The above info would maybe suggest to treat it as a fixed effect, since you only have 2 years. Buuuut... do you think the effect of year might vary depending on site? Maybe? One way to handle this might be to slightly expand your random effect to be for both site by years. You would say that each site x year combo could have a different survival with a mean of zero and standard deviation, sigma. This would require a 2-dimensional array for that random effect. In your second model, I see that you are trying to do this by creating a 2-dimensional array (which is good!), and this is why you get unique values for each site and year. But I still think you are treating that as a fixed effect, because you are basically estimating each site x year to have it's own survival, and not modeling the among site-by-year with a distribution, mean, and variance term that random effects involve.

As for other predictors, etc., my sense is always to get the base model right first, before then adding in the additional fixed-effects. Testing your main hypotheses of interest (fixed effects) is meaningless until the base model is robust, I think. So I think you are wise to try to sort out that model first. 

Anyway, just my $0.02! A lot here, and surely some of it is wrong. But hopefully it's helpful. Don't hesitate to reach out to me directly if you have more questions.

Best,

Brian

messages.subject: Re: Parameterizing nested hierarchy in survival model, fixed/random effects
parts:
Hey Stephanie,

Firstly, your current model isn't hierarchical, as you're not estimating the hyperparameters, which you have fixed at dlogis(3.5, 0.75). The difference between "fixed" and "random" effect is simply the prior: you're giving independent logistic(3.5, 0.75) priors for each site, whereas a random effect would estimate the mean and scale of the distribution, e.g.:

mu ~ dlogis(0, 1)
tau ~ dexp(1)
for (s in 1:7) {

phi.site[s] ~ dlogis(mu, tau)
}

Re: your question, I think what you're looking for is 7 site effects and 2 random year effects, so you produce the site-by-year random effect. I'd write it like this:

phi_bar ~ dlogis(0, 1)  # mean survival
phi_tau[1] ~ dexp(1)  # site-level scale
phi_tau[2] ~ dexp(1) # year-level scale
for (s in 1:7) {
phi_site[s] ~ dnorm(0, 1 / sqrt(phi_tau[1])

}
for (y in 1:2) {

phi_year[y] ~ dnorm(0, 1 / sqrt(phi_tau[2])
}

Then produce the survivals:

for (i in 1:n.nest) {
  for (t in (f[i]+1):k[i]) {

logit(phi[i,t-1]) <- phi_bar + phi_site[site[i]] + phi_year[year[i]]
  }
}

However, I can almost guarantee that sampling will be horrible with this centered parameterisation and so few sites/years. You should probably default to the non-centered parameterisation:
for (s in 1:7) {

phi_site[s] <- phi_tau[1] * phi_site_z[s]
  phi_site_z[s] ~ dnorm(0, 1)

}
for (y in 1:2) {

phi_year[y] <- phi_tau[2] * phi_year_z[y]
  phi_year_z[y] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
}

Re: sites nested in regions, you could easily add another random effect for each region:

for (r in 1:R) {
  phi_region[r] <- phi_tau[3] * phi_region_z[r]
  phi_region_z[r] ~ dnorm(0, 1)

}
for (i in 1:n.nest) {
for (t in (f[i]+1):k[i]) {

logit(phi[i,t-1]) <- phi_bar + phi_site[site[i]] + phi_region[region[i]] + phi_year[year[i]]
  }
}

However, these effects will be difficult to identify, especially with one two sites in one region. Ideally you'd be using sum-to-zero constraints (on all random effects), so you have a clearly defined intercept etc. Unfortunately JAGS doesn't allow this, but Stan now has really good sum-to-zero types. I wrote a bunch of Stan code for different mark-recapture models, and you could easily add this to the parameters block to make it all identified, where S is number of sites, K is number of years (I'd advise against using Y for anything other than data), and R is number of regions.

parameters{
  vector<lower=3> phi_tau;  // random effect scales
  sum_to_zero_vector[S] phi_site_z;  // site effects
  sum_to_zero_vector[K] phi_year_z;  // year effects
  sum_to_zero_vector[R] phi_region_z;  // regions effects
}

Then produce the random effects like this:

transformed parameters {
  vector[S] phi_site = phi_tau[1] * phi_site_z;
  // rest follows
}

Hope this helps!

Matt
